candidate.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication safety, contraindications and monitoring
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — edoxaban renal-function limitation
candidate.educational_objective: Identify the edoxaban NVAF limitation in clients with CrCl greater than 95 mL/min and question an unsafe prescription.

options.A: Administer edoxaban as prescribed because higher creatinine clearance improves its stroke-prevention efficacy
options.B: Question the prescription because current U.S. labeling states edoxaban should not be used for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation when CrCl is greater than 95 mL/min
options.C: Reduce the edoxaban dose by half because every CrCl above 95 mL/min requires dose reduction rather than a different anticoagulant
options.D: Hold all anticoagulation permanently because a high CrCl is a contraindication to anticoagulant therapy in general

candidate.rationale: Edoxaban has a boxed limitation for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: it should not be used when creatinine clearance exceeds 95 mL/min because efficacy for prevention of ischemic stroke was reduced compared with warfarin in this group. Renal function therefore must be assessed before initiation. This restriction is specific to edoxaban use for NVAF and does not mean anticoagulation itself is contraindicated.
candidate.source_claim_supported: For NVAF, edoxaban should not be used when CrCl exceeds 95 mL/min; renal function must be assessed before therapy.
candidate.source_locator: Boxed Warning; Sections 1.1, 2.1 and 5.1 — do not use for NVAF when CrCl >95 mL/min because of increased ischemic stroke risk versus warfarin
candidate.source_version_date: DailyMed updated July 10, 2025; labeling revised October 2023
candidate.stem: A client with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation has a new prescription for edoxaban. The calculated creatinine clearance is 108 mL/min. Which action should the nurse take?
